query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating approximately 2 at.% titanium (Ti) into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will promote grain-boundary segregation and the in situ formation of fine, ductile Ti-rich precipitates, which will arrest crack initiation and propagation. This microstructural refinement is expected to improve compressive strength (surpassing the 218 MPa benchmark from epoxy composites) while maintaining the large intrinsic caloric response (with less than a 10% reduction in ΔT).
generation.material_initial_state: The base (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of Ti (approximately 2 at.%) into the alloy composition during processing.
generation.conditions: Testing under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields, near the caloric phase-transition temperature, and under mechanical compression loading regimes where the original alloy tends to crack.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, ductile Ti-rich precipitates at the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Ti is expected to segregate to the grain boundaries during processing, promoting the nucleation of fine, ductile precipitates that improve grain-boundary cohesion and arrest crack propagation. This should enhance mechanical integrity without significantly altering the crystallographic features responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should achieve a compressive strength exceeding 218 MPa while maintaining a caloric temperature change (ΔT) within 10% of that of the base alloy.
generation.baseline: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with poor crack resistance and compressive strengths below or comparable to 218 MPa, albeit with a large caloric response.
generation.boundary: The effects are expected under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields, near the phase-transition temperature of the alloy, and during mechanical compression testing that previously caused cracking in the unmodified alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal Ti concentration and processing conditions may require adjustment. It is also uncertain whether the Ti addition might have subtle effects on the caloric response beyond the targeted <10% reduction.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples with 1, 2, and 3 at.% Ti additions using identical processing routes. Subject these samples to applied magnetic and pressure fields and perform standard mechanical compression tests while monitoring the phase-transition temperature range.
measurements: Compressive strength using standardized compression tests
Caloric temperature change (ΔT) under applied-field conditions
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM, SEM) to confirm Ti segregation and precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped samples do not exhibit a compressive strength significantly exceeding 218 MPa or if the caloric response (ΔT) decreases by more than 10% compared to the unchanged alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ]. frame.system: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy in its baseline state—that is, showing a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but suffering from poor mechanical integrity (i.e., it tends to crack).
frame.goal: To achieve the coexistence of robust structural integrity (enhanced mechanical strength and crack resistance) with high caloric performance.
frame.limitation: Under the currently tested conditions, the alloy cracks (poor integrity), and previous composite methods improved either strength or heat transport but not both concurrently, while preserving caloric response.
root_cause_cues: desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved
constraints: The intervention must be a single change (i.e., a single processing or compositional intervention)
It must not sacrifice the high caloric response of the original alloy
regime: Applied-field and pressure-field operational conditions that trigger the caloric effect
Temperature regimes around the phase‐transition temperature of the alloy
Mechanical loading (e.g., compression) that leads to cracking in the unmodified alloy
prior_attempts: Epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe composites that yielded compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents
Low-melting In composites that provided 48 MPa compressive strength and significantly increased thermal conductivity, but with trade-offs in strength
frame.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of a ductility-promoting element (for example, 1–3 at.% Ti or V) to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 system.
frame.mechanism: The added element is expected to segregate to grain boundaries during processing and promote the formation of fine, ductile precipitates. This in situ toughening is anticipated to arrest crack initiation and propagation without disturbing the matrix’s crystallographic features that drive the caloric effect. Thus, the microstructural refinement should boost compressive strength and integrity while retaining the intrinsic large caloric response.
frame.expected_outcomes: Relative to the unchanged alloy, the modified alloy should exhibit, for example, a compressive strength exceeding that of the 218 MPa epoxy-composite benchmark and maintain the caloric temperature change (ΔT) within an acceptable range (e.g., <10% reduction).
frame.boundary_conditions: Under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields that induce the caloric effect, over the temperature range where the phase transition occurs, and while undergoing standard mechanical compression tests that previously led to cracking.
frame.supporting_prior_evidence: Prior work in intermetallic systems and high-entropy alloys suggests that microalloying with elements such as Ti or V can enhance grain-boundary cohesion and induce ductile phase precipitation without significantly compromising functional properties. Similar strategies in MM′X compounds have led to improvements in mechanical properties, providing precedence for this approach.
frame.falsification_experiment: Prepare a series of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples with incremental additions (e.g., 1, 2, and 3 at.%) of the chosen element (Ti or V) using identical processing routes. Evaluate their compressive strengths and caloric responses under identical applied-field, pressure-field, and thermal cycling conditions. If the samples either do not show a significant improvement in strength (i.e., remain below or comparable to 218 MPa) or exhibit a reduction in the caloric effect by more than ~10% compared to the original alloy, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Over recent years, research on high‐entropy and MM′X materials has attempted to improve the mechanical performance of functional alloys through secondary phase formation or composite routes. Earlier studies using epoxy and low‐melting metal composites improved either compressive strength or thermal conductivity while keeping the caloric response acceptable; however, they introduced trade-offs (e.g., strength versus heat transport) and did not address the intrinsic microstructural weaknesses that lead to cracking. In related HEAs, very small compositional modifications—such as adding 0.5 at.% Hf or Mo—were used to induce fine, ductile precipitates and to improve grain-boundary cohesion without significantly altering the matrix phases that are responsible for functional behavior. This progression from external composite integration toward in situ microalloying suggests an increased focus on a controlled composition_change to directly refine the alloy’s microstructure.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved challenge is achieving robust structural integrity (improved compressive strength and crack resistance) while retaining the large intrinsic caloric response in (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38. Previous interventions have improved one property at the expense of another, and composite routes have not realized the coexistence of both high mechanical strength and caloric performance in a single-phase or uniformly processed material.
decision.lever: Introduce a minor addition (1–3 at.%) of a ductility-promoting element (e.g., Ti or V) into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy. This lever involves tuning the alloy composition to favor the segregation of the added element to the grain boundaries and promote the formation of fine, ductile precipitates during processing.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend observed in other high-entropy and MM′X systems where small compositional tweaks have led to in situ microstructural refinement and improved grain-boundary cohesion without compromising the primary functional phase. By leveraging prior evidence (e.g., from PMC7514651 and similar studies), which shows that microalloying can arrest crack initiation/propagation, the proposed intervention specifically targets the poor integrity of the alloy while aiming to keep the caloric effect within an acceptable range (<10% reduction). A decisive experiment would test a series of samples with 1–3 at.% Ti (or V) additions, evaluating their compressive strength and caloric response under the same applied-field, pressure-field, thermal, and mechanical loading conditions used in the original studies.
